a remark that only made sense on the card: the household name of Raya’s grandmother, declined in the libellī. A personal name cannot head a record or a term, and none of this card’s examples uses it; the family card (sermo entry-54) has Baba as Theo’s proavia. See the flags.
dropped.Babae, Babā: the declined forms of the household name Baba (same reason)

flags: Family or local references, carried over as the lead asked but worth a decision before the lexicon goes public: osoitsa (“our village”, the family’s home), antanhol (“the grandparents’ village”), and the Libellus III example in restaurant naming a local café (“Rādīcēs nōmine”, Raízes). Bali, Sofia, Lisbon, Sintra, Alfama, the Gare do Oriente and the Parque das Nações are public places and are kept as ordinary place records; the last two are headed by the names English uses for them, with the translations in “also”.

Dropped (see "dropped"): Baba, Babae f., “from Bulgarian baba, grandmother; the household name, declined in the libellī (Babae, Babā)”. It is a personal name, so it cannot head a record or a term, and nothing in this card uses it. If it should stay, its place is the family record that sermo entry-54 will become (Baba as proavia).

entry-542 says of medicus dentārius “Traupman has no word for it”, but Traupman has “dentist medicus dentārius” on pp. 63 and 302 (searchable text), as corpus entry-301 also says (Traupman 63). Kept as written in dentist; the comment should go.

entry-545 says of macellārius “L&S gives only the adjective, Val. Max.”, but Lewis & Short also gives the noun, “a meat-seller, victualler”, Varr. R.R. 3.2.11; 3.4.2; Suet. Caes. 26, Vesp. 19, as entry-431 says. Both cards’ citations are in grocer, with the wrong comment kept as written; period set to classical.

arcārius (cashier): entry-430 says “classically a treasurer”, entry-545 “in L&S a treasurer, late”. Lewis & Short marks the noun “(late Lat.)”: Vulg. Esth. 3.9, Rom. 16.23; Dig. 40.5.41. Both comments are kept; period set to late.

entry-542 says veterīnārius as a bare noun is late and classical Latin says medicus veterīnārius (Col.). Lewis & Short cites the noun from Columella itself (6.8.1; 7.5.14; 11.1.12) and the adjective with medicina, not medicus (Col. 7.3.16). Comment kept; period left late as the card has it, though L&S would make it classical.

entry-432 says L&S lists cuppēdō “only as a form of cupīdō”. Lewis & Short has a second cuppēdō, “a desire for delicacies, a tidbit, delicacy” (Forum Cupedinis, Varr. L.L.). It is still not a shop, so it stays “avoid” in cake-shop, but the reason needs rewording. Related: Traupman 174 and 357 give cuppedināria for “pastry shop”, the word the libellī use for a cake shop (the Libellus III and V examples in clothes-shop and restaurant), while entry-432 gives taberna cuppēdināria for a delicatessen (M-O) and taberna dulciāria for a cake shop. The two shops may want reconciling.

entry-429 prints dīvendō (short e) beside omnia dīvēndita sunt and vēndō, vēndere: one of them is probably wrong. Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked (dī-vendo, dĭtum). Both copied as printed (sold-out).

entry-231 prints Alfama, “indeclinable”, without a macron. The Latinitas standards (AGENTS.md §2, Jack 30 Oct) and the series bible write Alfāma, the long ā giving the Portuguese stress; the readers no longer use the name. Copied as printed.

entry-225 glosses piscātrīx “fishwife, fish seller”. Lewis & Short knows it only as “she that fishes” (rāna piscātrīx, Plin. 9.143), and Libellus IV says piscium vēnditrīx; so the sense is ours and the period is set to “ours”.
entry-225 calls taberna cāseāria “a cheesemonger’s shop (L&S, Dig.)”; Lewis & Short glosses the Digest’s taberna cāseāria (8.5.8.5) as a room “in which cheese was smoked and kept”.
dēnumerō, dēnumerāre (entry-227; Libellus IV nummōs dēnumerāvit) is not in Lewis & Short, which has only dī-numero, “count over”. Period set to modern (Traupman 129–131) until someone checks the OLD.
Traupman 131 is cited for vēneō, but the searchable text has vēneō on p. 130 (vēnālis is on 131). Kept as printed.

entry-233’s source line put “Lewis & Short: Bergomum” inside the Mediolanum link. milan keeps the link, labelled Mediolanum; bergamo cites Lewis & Short s.v. Bergomum without a link (no URL was invented). The card’s keywords also had “Malpensa”, which is not the airport of Libellus VI; not carried.

Overlaps with cards being converted elsewhere: corpus entry-301 (doctor, dentist, nurse, pharmacy, pharmacist, hospital, doctor’s surgery; it also says “we don’t use” pharmacopōla, which pharmacist keeps as an alternative after entry-542), corpus entry-308 (hairdresser, barber, barber’s shop, haircut), domus entry-421 (dry cleaner’s, fullō), domus entries 86, 264 and 273 (bath/bathroom balneum; lābrum as tub or washbasin), domus entry-87 (bookshelf; here bookcase), sermo entry-313 (babysitter/nanny gerula; midwife), sermo entry-547 (primary school, pupil), natura entry-278 (South America, with the same Traupman 202), natura entry-199 (clīvōsus, steep), culina entry-120 (shopping list, kilogram), culina entry-412 (parcel), vectura entry-217 (tickets: the tesserae aditiālēs example sits in museum).

Masculine and feminine forms that a card gives together (medicus; medica, minister; ministra, vīcīnus; vīcīna and the like) are two terms, both recommended, the feminine glossed “(woman)”. Synonyms joined by “or” or listed after the lead are alternatives.

Periods chosen where the card is silent (the later one when unsure): Bulgaria and Polōnia medieval; Anglicē medieval (British medieval documents); America renaissance (Waldseemüller, 1507); Americānus, Brasilia, Brasiliānus modern; Bulgaricē ours, like Lūsitānicē; Portus Cale late (Hydatius’ Portucale); Conimbrica medieval (the card says “a post-classical transfer of the name”); Serdica late (L&S cites only Cassiodorus); vestificus, vestifica post-classical (L&S cites only inscriptions); vēnditrīx, ēmptrīx post-classical (L&S: Digest); fullōnica as a shop post-classical (L&S: Dig. 39.3.3); cantātrīx late (L&S: Vulg.); ēmptum īre and fidē suā emere modern (Traupman; L&S has neither phrase); ancient names used for modern countries (Lūsitānia, Hispānia, Gallia) classical.

Classical words in a modern sense are “modern”: mūsēum (museum), bibliothēca (bookcase; L&S has only library), syngrapha (cheque), praecōnium (advertisement), centēsima (percent, cent), arca (till). Close classical senses stay classical: vīvārium (zoo), vigil (police officer), remissiō (discount).

Domain kept as urbs, though these belong elsewhere: spend the winter, bookcase (domus-structura), kilogram, scales and pound (culina, measures), primary school and pupil (sermo), bath and basin (domus).

One record per sense, so a shared word appears more than once: lībra in scales and pound, bibliothēca in library and bookcase, statiō vigilum in police station and fire station, thermae and balneae in spa and public baths, centēsima in percent and cent.
bookshop leads with taberna librāria (entry-432; Cic. Phil. 2.21; the Vatican lexicon) over entry-540’s librāria, which Lewis & Short does not have as a bookshop (only the bookseller, librārius).
menu takes Traupman’s index cibōrum (p. 72) as an alternative, since entry-433 points to it; list keeps the card’s comment on index rērum emendārum with a link to entry-120.
The obrigado note (Portuguese “thank you” from obligātus) is kept in portuguese because it explains the Libellus IV example; under the English–Latin rule it may not belong.
cafe gives Traupman’s cafēum; the coffee card (culina entry-33) prefers caffēa with ff for the drink.
